summary:
Puerto Rico is a United States territory and stands under the United States federal framework for entry, documents, federally funded care and federal custody; the findings below are the territory's own law, its own enforcement and its own institutions.

Ley Núm. 63 de 2025, the Law for the Protection of the Health and Wellbeing of Minors, was enacted in July 2025. It bars gender-affirming care for anyone under 21, withdraws public funding for that care, and penalises violations with a fixed 15-year prison term, a $50,000 fine per violation for legal persons, and permanent loss of medical licences for professionals. Article 4, the operative prohibition, is directed at medical institutions and health professionals: none may perform surgical interventions or medication treatments that alter sex biology under the pretext of gender transition or as part of gender-dysphoria treatment.

Article 3 defines the banned chemical and surgical practice more broadly than the operative clause. It expressly names the use of puberty blockers and sex hormones, including androgen blockers, oestrogen, progesterone or testosterone, when used to treat gender dysphoria, and it sets the protected class at anyone under 21. Article 6 penalises any person who violates the law's provisions.

The gap between a definition framed around patient use and an operative clause that restricts only providers leaves an unresolved question. Under ordinary criminal-law principles a successful prosecution of a visiting under-21 trans person for using their own lawfully prescribed hormones, or of a parent accompanying them, would almost certainly fail, and no test case had resolved the question at the time of writing. For an under-21 trans traveller the practical reading is that carrying and using prescribed hormone treatment on the island sits inside the law's literal definition of a banned practice, and that enforcement risk is harassment-shaped rather than conviction-shaped: questioning, detention or investigation by hostile officials, with the answer arriving only after the fact. The law's protected class is anyone under 21 and does not on its face reach patients 21 or older.

The law was pushed through non-public hearings and is written with deliberate vagueness, so doctors and affirming parents who facilitate hormone treatment or top surgery risk prosecution, a reach that extends to the accompanying parents of a travelling trans teenager. It mandates campaigns by the Education and Health departments on the risks of trans-affirming care. Health Secretary Víctor Ramos Parés proposed amendments that would have allowed puberty blockers and the continuation of existing hormone treatment; the text as enacted stands as the most restrictive care law in any United States jurisdiction according to the report documenting it. The Puerto Rico LGBTQ+ Federation announced plans to challenge the ban in court.

The ACLU of Puerto Rico urged Governor Jenniffer González Colón to veto Senate Bill 350, which it said criminalizes doctors and parents and creates two distinct categories of children divided by whether identity aligns with sex assigned at birth. Policy Counsel Lolimar Escudero Rodríguez stated that the bill allows parents to authorise treatment where a child's identity aligns with the sex assigned at birth and prohibits them the same right where it does not. Executive Director Annette Martínez Orabona said the measure discriminates against transgender people and denies the existence of trans children and youth. The bill was authored by Senate President Thomas Rivera Schatz and Senator Joanne Rodríguez Veve, passed both chambers in April, was returned for amendments suggested by Health Secretary Ramos Parés that the ACLU warned did not remedy the rights violations, and was re-approved and returned to the Governor on 28 June. Opposition was registered by the Puerto Rico College of Physicians and Surgeons, the Puerto Rico Psychology Association, the College of Social Work Professionals, the Puerto Rican Association of Professional Counseling, the Puerto Rico Bar Association and the LGBTQ+ Federation of Puerto Rico.

Puerto Rico amended its hate crime statutes in 2002 to include sexual orientation and gender identity as protected characteristics. The first hate crime charges in the territory's history were brought in 2020, after Sean Díaz de León and Juan Pagán Bonilla were charged in the murder of two transgender women on 22 April 2020; Bonilla confessed to the killings. In January 2021 Governor Pedro Pierluisi declared a state of emergency over ongoing murders, assaults and rape of transgender individuals on the island.

Anti-discrimination coverage is partial. The 2013 law that passed, Senate Bill 238, signed 29 May 2013, was amended in the House to apply only to employment discrimination, so public facilities, housing, transit and business transactions are not covered. An earlier bill, House Bill 1725, passed the House 43-6 in November 2009 with wider coverage, but the Senate held no hearings and took no action after Senate President Thomas Rivera Schatz said it would not be approved.

Marriage recognition for same-sex couples was won through federal court rather than local statute. The challenge was filed in March 2014 in the Ada Conde Vidal case, with intervention from Lambda Legal and Puerto Rico Para Todas, and in June 2014 four couples joined as plaintiffs, among them a former National Guard member and two couples already married in Canada in 2007 and in New York in 2012.

Consensual private sexual activity between adults is not criminalised. The Puerto Rico Supreme Court upheld the territory's sodomy ban in 2002; after the United States Supreme Court's 2003 ruling invalidated state and territorial sodomy statutes covering consensual private acts, Puerto Rico amended its Penal Code in 2004 to remove private, non-commercial sexual activity between consenting adults from the statute.
tangentialFactors: Legislative attempts to protect trans residents have repeatedly stalled on the island. In March 2019 the pro-statehood New Progressive Party caucus in the Puerto Rico House blocked a floor vote on Senate Bill 1000, which would have banned conversion therapy for minors, despite Senate passage and governor support; Senator Zoe Laboy, a co-sponsor, dissented publicly. In April 2019 Governor Ricardo Rosselló announced Senate Bill 1253 on religious freedom principles alongside Senate Bill 1254, a conversion-therapy ban carrying an exemption for clergy acting in a pastoral capacity. LGBT advocates, among them council president Johanne Velez Garcia, criticised the pairing as opening the door to refusals of service on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and on 13 June 2019 the governor asked lawmakers to withdraw both measures. A 2017 religious freedom bill that would have allowed public businesses to refuse service to LGBTQ people was vetoed by Rosselló in February 2018.
localsOnly:
The care ban withdraws public funding for gender-affirming treatment, which bears directly on how residents, rather than visitors, obtain care on the island.

The law mandates campaigns by the Education and Health departments on the risks of trans-affirming care, a measure that reaches trans students in the territory's schools.

House Bill 488, signed 29 May 2013, extended domestic violence protections to all households regardless of sexual orientation and gender identity.
outOfScopeNotes:
No court has resolved whether the definitional clause of Ley Núm. 63 de 2025 can reach a patient, or whether the statute is void for vagueness. The question is unresolved and no test case had been decided at the time of writing.

No territory-level corrections policy, dedicated unit or ruling on the housing of transgender inmates in Puerto Rico was located.

Reports differ on the surname of the health secretary who proposed amendments to the bill, rendering the attribution unresolved.
